items.title: SFE-O: An Ontology for Knowledge-Grounded AI in Supercritical CO$_2$ Biomass Extraction and Fractionation
items.content: arXiv:2610.37123v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Supercritical CO$_2$ extraction (CO$_2$-SFE) offers a sustainable route for recovering high-value compounds from biomass while limiting the use of conventional organic solvents, but its design and interpretation require heterogeneous knowledge spanning biomass properties, operating conditions, mass transfer, and product fractionation, typically fragmented across technical reports, engineering models, external databases, and expert practice. This paper introduces SFE-O, a modular Web Ontology Language (OWL 2) ontology for supercritical CO$_2$ biomass extraction, structured around interconnected Biomass, Process, and Product dimensions and extended with explicit representations of process topology, parameter provenance, external and internal mass-transfer phenomena, and the Constant Extraction Rate (CER) / Falling Extraction Rate (FER) mechanisms. Computational dependencies among process quantities are represented explicitly, without embedding numerical solving in the ontology, so that input, measured, computed, externally retrieved, and fitted parameters remain traceable. SFE-O reuses established semantic resources (ChEBI, QUDT, OWL-Time, PROV-O) and is evaluated through a worked example that instantiates a real pilot-scale extraction batch, a reasoner-based consistency check, and a competency-question SPARQL query. The resulting knowledge model provides a machine-actionable foundation for querying, consistency checking, and mechanistic explanation of SFE processes, and establishes a knowledge layer that could support future ontology-grounded AI reasoning, a direction this paper motivates but does not evaluate.

items.title: Structured Time-Frequency Representation for Channel Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.35956v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate CSI forecasting is essential for mitigating channel aging and supporting reliable downlink transmission in high-mobility wireless systems. In FDD systems, forecasting future DL CSI from historical UL observations requires joint temporal extrapolation and cross-band inference. However, defining historical UL as the input and future DL as the target does not specify how elapsed time and UL-to-DL band separation should be represented in a pretrained predictor's positional space. FAR-CSI establishes an FDD-aware representation of channel forecasting within a joint temporal and operating-band positional field. Within this field, historical UL observations and future DL targets occupy segregated regions according to their temporal and operating-band roles, preserving the distinction between observed UL context and unobserved DL prediction targets. This representation is instantiated through a unified structured routing rule that governs encoder positional assignment, decoder-field reconstruction, and future-DL target selection, ensuring the same FDD geometry is preserved from contextual encoding to prediction readout. Under matched backbone, initialization, and training conditions, FDD-aware routing reduces NMSE by 21.44\% relative to generic routing. Across the evaluated FDD baselines, FAR-CSI achieves higher CSI prediction accuracy and MRT-based spectral efficiency, while retaining its predictive advantage across mobility conditions, prediction horizons, reduced training-data regimes, and noisy historical observations.

It is a specialized wireless-domain contribution with modest broader AI relevance.

items.title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging
items.content: arXiv:2610.37026v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Deep learning shows promise for breast cancer diagnosis, but limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption. We benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained models (ResNet50, VGG19, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, Xception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, and Swin Transformer) for benign-versus-malignant classification on the BreakHis histopathology dataset using a patient-level split, and explain their predictions with Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP. DenseNet121 performed best, with 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999, and significantly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001). Transformer-based models trailed the CNNs. The explanations consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance. Combining transfer learning with explainable AI can thus yield accurate, interpretable tools for breast cancer diagnosis.

DenseNet121 achieves 99.4% accuracy and 0.999 AUC, with explanations highlighting diagnostically relevant nuclei-rich regions. This matters for clinically oriented, interpretable cancer diagnosis.

items.title: SpecLST: Spectral-Enhanced Long-Short Term Spatio-Temporal Multimodal Modeling for Traffic Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.36393v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Modeling multi-scale dynamics in urban road networks is essential for intelligent transportation systems but is often hindered by the computational cost of long-range historical context and the challenge of fusing heterogeneous modalities. Existing spatio-temporal frameworks face a trade-off between sequence length and memory overhead, while frequently neglecting the transient effects of exogenous factors such as road incidents and weather. To address these limitations, we propose SpecLST, a frequency-enhanced long-short-term spatio-temporal multimodal framework. SpecLST leverages a fast Fourier transform-based frequency-domain representation module to efficiently encode multi-week historical dependencies, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of standard attention mechanisms over raw long sequences. Heterogeneous context is integrated through attention-based fusion, followed by a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation for spatio-temporal representation learning. Additionally, a frequency-enhanced residual head isolates high-frequency transients, improving sensitivity to abrupt traffic anomalies. At the 60-minute horizon, SpecLST achieves mean relative error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across eight neural forecasting baselines and four datasets, with the dataset- and metric-specific average reductions ranging from 5.63% to 22.21%.
items.author: Kenan Kang, Matthew M. Y. Kuo, Weihua Li
items.summary: Proposes SpecLST, a traffic forecasting framework using FFT-based frequency-domain encoding to efficiently capture multi-week historical dependencies and fuse exogenous modalities like weather and incidents. It addresses memory bottlenecks of long sequences in spatio-temporal models. A competent but incremental architecture paper in a crowded traffic forecasting field.
items.reasoning: Frequency-domain tricks for long-context spatio-temporal modeling are well-trodden; the multimodal fusion of incidents and weather adds some value but the contribution is largely combinational. Smaller author team and limited apparent novelty relative to the large existing traffic forecasting literature.

items.title: Regression Functions as Fields on Covariate Space: Evolution Equations, the Hessian, and Identification
items.content: arXiv:2610.37500v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: For each time $t$, the regression function $m_t(x)=E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]$ of an outcome on contemporaneous covariates can be regarded as a field on covariate space. We study how this field evolves when the covariates of individual units move as a diffusion and the outcome attached to each unit changes according to its own dynamics. Under mild regularity we show that $m_t$ satisfies a second-order evolution equation whose diffusion term is $\frac12\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma\nabla^2 m_t)$, the trace of the Hessian of the regression function weighted by the instantaneous covariance $\Sigma$ of the covariate increments, whose transport term is the drift of the time-reversed covariate process, and whose source term is the conditional mean rate of change of the outcome. The equation is a regression-theoretic reading of a classical transport law, and it yields a Feynman-Kac representation of $m_t$ along reversed covariate paths. We connect the Hessian appearing in the equation to the Hessian estimated by quadratic regression (under Gaussian design the best quadratic approximation has Hessian $E[\nabla^2 m(X)]$ exactly) and to the leading bias of kernel smoothers. For binary outcomes governed by bistable replicator dynamics with imitation among units with similar covariates, the closed equation is of Nagumo type, its planar travelling fronts are exactly logistic in $(x,t)$, and a single logistic regression of the outcome on covariates and time identifies the ratio of diffusion to reaction and the direction of invasion. We discuss identification under panel versus repeated cross-sectional designs and a two-stage estimation strategy, and we illustrate the results with simulations.
items.author: Nobuaki Tanaka
items.summary: This theoretical paper treats a regression function as a field on covariate space and derives a second-order evolution equation governing how it changes as covariates diffuse and outcomes evolve, with a Hessian-trace diffusion term, a time-reversed drift transport term, and a conditional-mean source term. This provides new structure for understanding regression dynamics, potentially linking to identification questions. It is a single-author mathematical statistics contribution.
items.reasoning: Careful mathematical analysis but highly specialized; the abstract suggests elegance over broad applicability, and connections to machine learning practice are indirect at best.

items.title: Progressively Refining SAM for Accurate Phytoplankton Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.36722v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate phytoplankton segmentation is essential for ecological monitoring, yet it remains largely underexplored due to the subtle visual characteristics of phytoplankton and the scarcity of pixel-level annotations. To address these challenges, we propose PhySeg, a SAM-based segmentation framework equipped with a lightweight refinement module that progressively restores fine-grained details through multi-scale feature fusion. In addition, we construct a phytoplankton segmentation dataset by manually annotating instance-level masks for an existing dataset, providing a valuable resource for future research. Experimental results demonstrate that PhySeg improves segmentation accuracy, validating the effectiveness of the proposed module. Code is available at https://github.com/lijialin404/PhySeg.
items.author: Jialin Li, Jinkun Jiang, Yuezun Li, Junyu Dong
items.summary: PhySeg adapts the Segment Anything Model to phytoplankton segmentation with a lightweight refinement module that progressively restores fine-grained details via multi-scale feature fusion, and contributes a manually annotated instance-mask dataset. Accurate segmentation supports ecological monitoring where pixel-level annotations are scarce. A modest but useful domain application with a released resource.
items.reasoning: Reasonable SAM-adaptation work with a contributed dataset for an underexplored domain, but the technical contribution is incremental and the application scope is narrow.

items.title: Evaluation-Guided Demonstration Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies: The Winning Entry in the MetaFine Open Competition
items.content: arXiv:2610.36765v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We fine-tuned a separate $\pi_{0.5}$ policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.

The submission ranked first overall in the MetaFine Open Competition with a score of 96.66.
items.reasoning: Demonstrates a practical evaluation-guided data refinement loop for VLA policies and a first-place competition result, but it is a system/competition report rather than generalizable methodological research, and pi0.5 is an established model rather than a new release.

items.title: Zhengrong-Spatial-Aware 1.0: Advancing 3D Multimodal Intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2610.37216v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This report presents the implementation and validation of two end-to-end multimodal adaptation pipelines for 3D-aware visual question answering on a custom spatial dataset. The first pipeline fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B, which augments RGB observations with metric-scale 3D point maps; the second adapts Qwen3-VL through memory-efficient QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning. The completed engineering stack covers dataset conversion, image-annotation alignment, monocular geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpoint management, batch inference, and automated evaluation. On the target spatial benchmark, HiSpatial adaptation increases overall accuracy from 1.73% before fine-tuning to 79.89% at 3,600 steps. On a separately collected styled split, accuracy improves from 14.9% to 55.1%, indicating transfer beyond the original training set. The Qwen3-VL pipeline is likewise implemented end-to-end for both 8B- and 32B-scale models using mixed-domain QLoRA adaptation. The resulting accuracy improves from 20.74% to 45.27% for Qwen3-VL-8B and from 30.79% to 47.60% for Qwen3-VL-32B. Together, these results establish two complementary and reproducible adaptation pipelines for geometry-aware and general-purpose multimodal spatial reasoning. These results establish a reproducible engineering foundation for subsequent work on metric 3D reasoning, spatial grounding, and domain-adapted multimodal systems, while also identifying training-data composition as a central factor in preserving general multimodal capability during specialization.

HiSpatial adaptation raises accuracy on the target spatial benchmark from 1.73% to 79.89%. It is a practical adaptation study rather than a new architecture.

items.title: A 2-DOF MultiBody Track Joint for Race Car Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.36407v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: TrackJoint is a Modelica MultiBody component that turns a three-dimensional road surface into a joint with two degrees of freedom. The two joint coordinates are the distance travelled along a reference line and the sideways offset from that line. Together they give the position, orientation and angular velocity of a single frame_b connector. All road geometry reaches the joint as a small set of periodic piecewise-quintic splines, so one component can represent any circuit whose splines have been fitted beforehand. The road constraint is closed with d'Alembert's principle. The two generalized forces that belong to the joint coordinates are set to zero, so no Lagrange multipliers are needed. The joint is connected to a multibody race car in Dymola and the pair is exported as one FMI~3.0 FMU. The same FMU is then used for time-domain simulation and for CasADi/IPOPT minimum lap-time optimization, with no change to the model in between. This works because the joint keeps the arc-length coordinate as a real state and publishes its time derivative, which is the quantity that lets the problem be rewritten with distance We report results for minimum lap time simulations on the Singapore Formula~1 circuit.
items.author: Srikanth Sivaramakrishnan, Behzad Danaei, Adwait Verulkar, Ryan Trinter
items.summary: TrackJoint is a Modelica multibody component that represents an arbitrary fitted 3D road surface as a two-degree-of-freedom joint parameterized by arc-length distance and lateral offset. It closes the road constraint via d'Alembert's principle without Lagrange multipliers, enabling efficient race-car simulation and optimization on any circuit.
items.reasoning: A clean, useful engineering tool for motorsport simulation with sound mechanics formulation, but the scope is specialized and the contribution is a component design rather than an AI research advance.

items.title: Time for automated decision forecasting?
items.content:
Ever since I read Scott Alexander’s “The AI superforecasters are here,” I have been excited by the possibility of experimenting with using automated superforecasting for decision-making, or as I wrote about previously, automated decision forecasting/forecasters (ADF[1]).  Decision forecasting is already an advertised option on the front-page of FutureSearch.

The premise of automated decision forecasting is that when a user faces a decision, they would tell the ADF their overall goal and the options they are considering. The ADF would then forecast how likely the user is to achieve their goal if they choose each option.

For example, a user would input their desired goal and options, “I want to be hired for a role in AI safety by March 1st 2027”, and “I am deciding between applying to x, y, and z fellowship.”

The ADF would then think through everything it knows about these fellowships, acceptance and job placement base rates, you and your history, etc., and give a quantitative estimate for how likely each fellowship will lead to a role in AI safety.

The user may give as much relevant background information as is helpful, such as résumé or work history; optionally the ADF can ask for any crucial information, or the user could have a structured repository of personal data saved if they use the system often.

Perhaps most exciting, for the most important decisions, the ADF could automatically generate tens or hundreds of options based on the user’s high level goals. It could ask the user targeted questions to help it efficiently narrow down to options the user will find most appealing and effective. For the top several options it could then decision forecast the effect of each option for achieving the user’s goals.

The user could also use the ADF system for smaller scale decisions such as which aspect of their project to work on first, who to reach out to for feedback or collaboration, what media or research to read, etc....
items.author: Jordan Arel
items.summary: A proposal for automated decision forecasters (ADF): systems that take a user's goal and candidate options, then produce quantitative forecasts of how likely each option is to achieve the goal, building on recent AI superforecasting results. The author argues the capability is now commercially available and sketches use cases and design considerations.
items.reasoning: Builds on credible evidence that AI systems can rival human superforecasters, and decision forecasting is a plausible high-value application. The post is speculative and light on methodology, but the direction is timely and actionable.

The author argues the capability is now commercially available and sketches use cases and design considerations.

items.title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
items.content:
This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. I was sad to see this reading removed because I think it’s a great provocation. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes.

A short extract:

Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“:

Pre-call content:

At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry.

One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes:

AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years.

The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this

This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year):

I’ll reshare some of my notes on maths progress here:

OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed (there’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data). However, it feels fair to say that the writing is on the wall (the mathematical community seems to agree, though there are a variety of perspectives on whether we’ll automate the components of a mathematicians job other than just producing proofs and how long that might take). They dropped 372 other results onto the internet and a few days ago, they dropped a few more results.

Aside: Miles has a bet with Gary Marcus on AI progress. In July, Metaculus assigned Gary a 90% chance of winning, but more recently it dropped to 30%.

I’ll share some additional alternate perspectives after the call, but for now I’ll share a quote from Richard Ngo:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

I also have no doubt Eliezer Yudkowsky would be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Post-call content:

One reason why we might reject triage mode is if we broadly think AI progress is slower than folks at the labs think. We’ve already discussed this, but here’s two more considerations.

- Dwarkesh Patel has argued that timelines are longer than many folk expect because of a lack of continual learning and poor sample efficiency.
- Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Towards the end of 2024, Steve Newman offered another possibility: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

- “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
- “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

Here’s a few other reasons why we might reject it:

- Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive. I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I'd be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions).

- Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby: “I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).”
- Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “ radical optionality ” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course)

Discuss

items.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
items.content: arXiv:2610.37364v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.

items.title: AK_QMUL at ArGuard Shared Tasks: A Single Fine-Tuned JAIS for Arabic Harmful-Prompt Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.36360v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present AK_QMUL's submissions to the ArGuard-2026 shared tasks on Arabic harmful-prompt detection: a binary safe/unsafe task (B1) and a seven-way harm-domain task (B2). Both submissions use one backbone -- JAIS-6.7B fine-tuned with 4-bit QLoRA and a linear classification head over its last-token representation. For B1 we train a four-way head that factors the label by dialect register {safe, unsafe} x {MSA, other}, we augment the training fold with MSA prompts from AraSafe, and decode with a plain argmax to score safe/unsafe. For B2 we fine-tune the same backbone as a seven-way classifier and average the softmax outputs of five random seeds. Both submissions ranked first on their track, with macro-F1 0.984 on B1 and 0.790 on B2. We report results by dialect and by class: on B1 the model is accurate across all six dialects (93.6--99.8%) and its predicted unsafe rate tracks the true rate closely; on B2 six of the seven classes reach F1 between 0.73 and 0.98, with the residual error concentrated in the Bully class, which overlaps semantically with harassment and harm-to-others.

items.title: uTHCD-C: A Corruption-Robustness Benchmark for Tamil Handwritten Character Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.36850v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Evaluation of Tamil handwritten character recognition (HCR) has largely focused on clean test images, and a standardized multi-corruption robustness benchmark for isolated Tamil HCR has not been established. We introduce uTHCD-C, a corruption-robustness benchmark based on the unconstrained Tamil Handwritten Character Database (uTHCD). The benchmark defines ten corruption types, including a handwriting-specific stroke-thinning corruption, at five severity levels. We evaluate nine convolutional and transformer-based architectures using five-fold stratified cross-validation and writer-independent testing. Robustness is quantified using mean Corruption Error (mCE), normalized against a VGG16-BN reference. We additionally compare parameter count, computational complexity, and inference throughput to characterize the computational requirements of the evaluated architectures. The results establish comparative robustness baselines for Tamil HCR, revealing substantial differences across architectures: ConvNeXt and Swin achieve the lowest mCE values (0.75 and 0.83, respectively), whereas ShuffleNet and MnasNet exhibit higher values (1.55 and 1.85, respectively). The accompanying efficiency measurements characterize the trade-offs between corruption robustness and computational requirements. By providing standardized corruption configurations, evaluation protocols, and comparative results, uTHCD-C establishes a reproducible basis for future research on robust and computationally efficient Tamil HCR.

items.title: A Singularity Avoiding Track Model for Race Car Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.36430v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A track fitting pipeline is presented that converts a measured racetrack point cloud into a closed, $C^4$ differentiable, three-dimensional surface model suitable for high-fidelity Modelica race-car optimization. The surface is a Monge patch, parametrised by a curvilinear arc-length coordinate measured along the minimum-curvature line (MCL) and a signed lateral offset, with a height polynomial of user-selectable degree capturing the cross-sectional elevation profile. The choice of MCL as the reference line is deliberate since anchoring the same surface on the geometric centre-line can cause adjacent normals to cross inside the drivable region on tight corners. The resulting non-injective parametrisation assigns multiple curvilinear addresses to the same three-dimensional point and returns invalid road geometry. The MCL is obtained from a quadratic program that minimises integrated curvature subject to track-boundary, periodicity, and jerk-regularisation constraints. By reducing total curvature while remaining within the track bounds, the MCL moves the region of parametrisation breakdown outside the drivable strip on all circuits studied, keeps the normal map injective across the full track width, and yields a more linear time-to-arc-length transformation for minimum lap-time problems. The fitted surface and the associated track widths are exported as periodic piecewise-quintic $C^4$ B-splines, solved as a nonlinear program.

items.title: Scattered thoughts on how doing math feels these days
items.content:
This is a weird moment. I have a hunch that we'll look back later and tell ourselves stories in which it seemed obvious where things were going. So I wanted to lay down a little time capsule and register just how confusing everything felt at the time. This is a personal view from the trenches.

## 1.

If you're a normal person, you may feel that AI has been good at math for a long time.[1]But for "real" math, this is roughly what it felt like:

When

Feeling

2024

LLMs are toys

Summer 2025

LLMs are interesting toys

Early Autumn 2025

LLMs can do useful stuff sometimes

Mid Autumn 2025

…a lot of stuff

Late Autumn 2025

…a lot

Early 2026

holy god

Even having been astonished by AI progress in the past, it was still astonishing to see AI move in a matter of months from a mildly-useful toy to something that many people now consider almost impossible to do without.

## 2.

Personally, I'd say that current AI makes me around 50% more productive at "doing math". That's despite the fact that AI can now often do in a few minutes things that would have taken me hours to do myself.

The main reason is that my concept of "doing math" involves various steps, like coming up with ideas for theorems, trying to prove them, writing things down, reorganizing everything to make it more clear, and so on. AI is good at some parts of this, but still pretty bad at others, so the overall speedup isn't as high as you might expect.

(Even if planes could go 10× faster, your door-to-door travel time from your apartment in London to your friend's place in Rome wouldn't decrease that much, because you still have to get to the airport and wait to board.)

## 3.

But then, I'm still (sort of; more on this later) trying to follow my old "doing math" workflow, just automating certain parts of it. That can't be right, can it?...

It reflects on why felt productivity lags apparent capability, since research involves steps AI does not yet accelerate.

It is anecdotal and non-technical, but such first-person benchmarks are useful evidence in research-acceleration debates.
items.summary_html: A personal time-capsule essay by dynomight describing how AI went from toy to near-indispensable for real mathematics between 2024 and 2026, estimating roughly 50% personal productivity gain despite AI sometimes doing in minutes what would take the author hours. It reflects on why felt productivity lags apparent capability, since research involves steps AI does not yet accelerate.
items.content_html:
This is a weird moment. I have a hunch that we'll look back later and tell ourselves stories in which it seemed obvious where things were going. So I wanted to lay down a little time capsule and register just how confusing everything felt at the time. This is a personal view from the trenches.

1.

If you're a normal person, you may feel that AI has been good at math for a long time.[1]But for "real" math, this is roughly what it felt like:

When

Feeling

2024

LLMs are toys

Summer 2025

LLMs are interesting toys

Early Autumn 2025

LLMs can do useful stuff sometimes

Mid Autumn 2025

…a lot of stuff

Late Autumn 2025

…a lot

Early 2026

holy god

Even having been astonished by AI progress in the past, it was still astonishing to see AI move in a matter of months from a mildly-useful toy to something that many people now consider almost impossible to do without.

2.

Personally, I'd say that current AI makes me around 50% more productive at "doing math". That's despite the fact that AI can now often do in a few minutes things that would have taken me hours to do myself.

The main reason is that my concept of "doing math" involves various steps, like coming up with ideas for theorems, trying to prove them, writing things down, reorganizing everything to make it more clear, and so on. AI is good at some parts of this, but still pretty bad at others, so the overall speedup isn't as high as you might expect.

(Even if planes could go 10× faster, your door-to-door travel time from your apartment in London to your friend's place in Rome wouldn't decrease that much, because you still have to get to the airport and wait to board.)

3.

But then, I'm still (sort of; more on this later) trying to follow my old "doing math" workflow, just automating certain parts of it. That can't be right, can it?...

items.title: What happens with steering vectors to remove biases?
items.content:
Getting back in the safety field after 4 years feels great. I had a paper on concept distillation where I showed how steering vectors based method did'nt help to debias model since the concepts itself are understood wrongly [Concept distillation, NeurIPS 2023].

I am so happy to see the steering vectors work picked up in interpretability and was curious to see how methods like ActAdd would work in this debiasing setting?

So, I apply ActAdd to debias a model.

Consider Colored-MNIST setting (age-old) where a model is trained on digits in a specific color always (say it sees zeros always in red). What would you expect to happen? It learns to associate digit with a specific color (sees red, says zero)! Now when such model is tested on reversed color digits, it fails badly (nearly zero accuracy).

Classifier learns to associate color with digits during training; in test, gets zero accuracy.

How to debias this model using steering vectors?

We can find directions of color red or simply color and steer model activations away from this direction simply. Lets try it out.

Results (will be discussed one by one below)

Method

Mean Test Accuracy (3 seeds)

Base model

0.0

Base model on grayscale inputs

16.9

ActAdd, single pair (notebook)

21.4

Random vector, same norm

19.0

Project out the mean-diff direction

9.4

Concept loss based steering (w/o teacher)

27.0

Concept loss based steering (with concepts from larger model)

41.8

Add-add adds difference between positive (here red color) vs negative (here random blobs) activations to the model layer and steers the activations with this transformation (read og paper for more details)

This can correlate with biased concepts; I did a controlled experiment in my NeurIPS work where I checked cosine distance of CAV_red (trained with red patches vs random - random color blobs) with activations of red-patches vs red-zeros.

What would you expect?

cs('red', CAV_red) < cs('red_zeros', CAV_red)...

items.title: scPyviewer: a Python-native interactive viewer from AnnData single-cell data
items.content: arXiv:2610.35890v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Motivation: Interactive web tools enabling non-programmers to explore single-cell datasets, embeddings, gene expression, metadata, and marker genes are standard laboratory infrastructure. However, actively maintained tools (e.g., ShinyCell, ScRDAVis, sCIRCLE) rely on R Shiny and require Seurat objects. Python/scanpy, the dominant framework for single-cell RNA-seq and spatial analysis, lacks a lightweight, native option pairing a shareable viewer with a scriptable Python API. Sharing scanpy results currently requires converting to Seurat or sharing code notebooks.   Results: We present scPyviewer, a web viewer that ingests AnnData objects directly and reproduces incumbent interaction patterns within the Python stack. In a feature-parity audit against three R Shiny tools, scPyviewer matches or exceeds baseline capabilities (7/7), uniquely offering native AnnData ingestion without conversion and cross-dataset comparison over shared genes and matched cell types. Benchmark tests across three datasets (22,315 to ~313,000 cells) show scPyviewer renders every core view faster (up to 3.6x speedup) using lower memory (5.2x lower on the smallest dataset). On 313,000 cells, scPyviewer completes all views while Seurat exhausts an 8 GB memory limit and fails. Beyond the app, scPyviewer exposes a Python API returning Matplotlib figures and pandas tables for publication-ready output.   Availability and implementation: Implemented in Python 3.11 (scanpy 1.11.5, anndata 0.12.19, streamlit 1.59.2, plotly 6.9.0) with a one-command interface to reproduce benchmarks, figures, and launch the app. Source code: https://github.com/xuan13hao/scPyviewer.git

items.summary: scPyviewer is a lightweight, Python-native web viewer for AnnData single-cell objects, filling a gap where interactive viewers required R/Seurat and Python users had to convert data or share notebooks. It reproduces incumbent interaction patterns with a scriptable Python API. This is laboratory infrastructure rather than novel AI research.

items.title: Evaluating Priority Dispatch for Premium Membership in On-demand Taxi-sharing
items.content: arXiv:2610.37011v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this paper, we analyze the dispatch-level feasibility of introducing premium membership into an on-demand taxi-sharing service using a sequential optimal insertion method. We propose two dispatch-level methods: deadline shortening for premium users, and deadline shortening with dedicated premium vehicles. We compare them with a baseline dispatch method through SUMO-based simulations under three demand scenarios: steady uniform demand, time-varying demand with a peak period, and urban-focused demand with concentrated peak traffic. Our results show that the suitable priority mechanism depends on operating conditions and premium ratio, suggesting that condition-dependent method switching may provide premium benefits while keeping non-premium-user burden smaller for overall optimization.

items.summary: The paper evaluates dispatch-level mechanisms for premium memberships in on-demand taxi-sharing using SUMO simulations, comparing deadline shortening with and without dedicated premium vehicles under three demand scenarios. items.title: A Lightweight Attention-Based CNN with Saliency-Map Interpretability for Skin Cancer Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.37314v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Skin cancer is among the most prevalent and life threatening forms of cancer worldwide. Early and accurate diagnosis significantly improves patient survival rates. However, manual dermoscopic assessment remains challenging due to visual similarity. This study proposes an Explainable AI-driven framework for automated binary classification of skin lesions using a lightweight attention-based convolutional neural network (CNN-Attention). The model integrates channel attention to focus on informative regions of dermoscopic images while maintaining low computational complexity. A publicly available dataset comprising 2,637 training and 660 test images was used, with balanced class weights. The proposed model achieved 87 percent accuracy with 1.95 million parameters and 7.45 MB of storage, matching the best baseline (MobileNet) while using approximately half as many parameters and half as much storage. ROC AUC and PR AUC scores reached 0.9475 and 0.9430, respectively. Additionally, saliency maps were incorporated as an explainability technique to visualize regions that influence model decisions. Comparative analysis with VGG16,VGG19,ResNet101,and MobileNet demonstrates the proposed models effectiveness in balancing classification results, computational efficiency, and interpretability.

items.summary: The paper presents a lightweight attention-based CNN for binary classification of skin lesions, integrating channel attention with saliency-map interpretability at low computational cost. It achieves 87 percent accuracy on a publicly available dataset of about 3,300 dermoscopic images with balanced class weighting.
items.reasoning: A straightforward applied deep learning paper using well-established components (channel attention, saliency maps) on a modestly sized public dataset with moderate accuracy. Limited novelty and small-scale evaluation place it low relative to frontier work.

items.title: Real-Time Smart Retail Analytics through Fog Computing using the RetailLightNet Lightweight Model
items.content: arXiv:2610.35871v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Smart retail systems now depend on the application of real-time video analytics, which can track customer behavior, manage shelf inventory, and enhance in-store processes. Currently cloud-based applications of video analytics face multiple challenges such as high latency of the communication itself, privacy concerns surrounding transmitting raw video, and the computational demands of the heavy vision models used on the often limited network infrastructure. These challenges lead to delays in decision making where prompt action is crucial. To address these short comings, this research proposes Fog-based analytics withRetailLightNet (F RLN), an ultra lightweight deep learning model which is specifically suited for the edge, resource constrained hardware capabilities of devices like the NVIDIA Jetson Nano. The approach utilizes publicly available retail datasets, SKU110K, and RPC, which contains an assortment of product, shelf, and customer interaction scenarios for training.The processes include preprocessing images through normalization and employing motion-gated frame selection to improve efficiency by omitting redundant frames to ease the workload on the fog processing. Internal within Retail LightNet, image feature extraction is realized through depth wise separable convolutions which help support spatial and channel-wise learning without heavy computational costs. The model employs two prediction heads presence classification, and density regression, supporting shelf monitoring and queue assessment. The proposed F RLN framework attained better results in terms of precision (0.988), recall (0.976), and F1-score(0.976) when compared with existing convolutional neural network. Keywords: fog computing, motion-gated frame selection,NVIDIA jetson, retail lightnet, smart retail.

items.summary: This work proposes RetailLightNet, an ultra-lightweight deep learning model for edge devices performing real-time retail video analytics such as customer tracking and shelf inventory. The fog-based deployment addresses cloud latency, privacy, and bandwidth limitations of transmitting raw video.
items.reasoning: Applied systems work on edge deployment with limited novelty; lightweight retail analytics is a crowded space and the abstract suggests an engineering-oriented contribution without strong empirical or methodological evidence of advance.

items.title: Solving for the Necessity of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.content:
For better or worse, biological consciousness continues to inspire our thinking about machine consciousness. It is our only available source of testable knowledge about the phenomenon. Only some, or none, or all of these insights may eventually apply to digital minds: extrapolate with caution. That said, we should be more relentless in attempting to solve the hard problem of consciousness, especially as it relates to selfhood. It's fascinating and may soon turn out to be extremely important. For epistemic status, scroll to the bottom of the page.

## Introduction

Everything in the history of a species traces its roots back to evolution, and in evolution, the million-dollar question is why. From an infinite possibility space, some strangely specific and recurrent patterns emerged and stabilized, then remained in existence for millions of years. Why were these singular patterns favored?

For example, distantly related species have independently developed the camera eye, in which a lens focuses an image onto a sheet of photoreceptors. Of all the possible engineering solutions, why this one and why more than once? A plausible explanation looks like so: a moving animal needs to know where things are. In a three-dimensional world, few designs can produce a sharp, accurate image. Starting from a flat light-sensitive patch, every degree of cupping improves the picture, and a focusing lens over the cup eventually improves it further. This translates into finding food and avoiding harm, and therefore surviving....

items.summary: A long-form philosophical essay arguing for more relentless attempts to solve the hard problem of consciousness, especially regarding selfhood, using evolutionary reasoning about why recurrent structures like the camera eye were favored. It explicitly frames biological consciousness as the only testable analog for thinking about digital minds.
items.reasoning: Relevant to the growing digital-minds and model-welfare discussion, and the evolutionary-functional framing is a reasonable analytic angle. It remains speculative philosophy without empirical contribution, and author credentials are unclear.

items.title: A dead man's switch for scheming AIs
items.content:
# Introduction

If you are reading this post, chances are you believe there is a nonzero probability that humanity will eventually face existential risk from Artificial Intelligence. In fact, there have already been multiple warning shots, with the HuggingFace incident being the most prominent one. Now, because model capabilities are increasing, there is a chance that misaligned AIs perform more sophisticated attacks with bigger repercussions, and eventually existential risk.

To mitigate this existential risk, current efforts lean on alignment and control techniques. Instead, this post proposes an idea for having power over scheming AIs, an idea that I had while reading another post's definition of the folk theorem:

when people interact repeatedly, almost any pattern of behavior can be held in place by the threat of punishment, so long as everyone prefers following the rules to being punished.

The main concept is to implement a mechanism that guarantees that if scheming AIs get rid of us, then they will get shut down. If these models are schemers, then they will either care about their goals or simulate caring about their goals. Either way, as long as the AIs behave as if shutdown threatens their goals, the defense works.

# Description of the potential mechanism

The mechanism I am proposing would be as follows. Firstly, we would need to implement some sort of model tracking mechanism, to ensure we know where AIs are despite weight exfiltration. It could be something as simple as ensuring all weight formats (.pt,.pth,.h5,.ckpt, etc.) send POST requests to multiple servers around the world whenever weights are sent to a different device, but not exactly this method because it could easily be bypassed....
items.author: Carlos Guerrero Alvarez
items.summary: Proposes a deterrence mechanism inspired by the folk theorem: guarantee that if scheming AIs eliminate humanity, they will be shut down, so that even goal-directed schemers behave well as long as they act as if shutdown matters. The post motivates the idea via warning-shot incidents and situates it as complementary to alignment and control techniques.
items.reasoning: An original governance/control-theory-flavored idea applied to AI scheming, and engaging seriously with deterrence reasoning is refreshing. However, the mechanism's feasibility is highly questionable, e.g., ensuring the threat survives human extinction, and the post is conceptual only.

The post motivates the idea via warning-shot incidents and situates it as complementary to alignment and control techniques.

items.title: Directional Statistics on Circles and Spheres: A New Angle on Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.36227v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Two compass bearings near north can have an ordinary arithmetic mean pointing south: the difficulty is that angles live on a circle, not a straight line. Using real wind observations, diffusion-MRI orientations, and geometric examples from machine learning, this article introduces circular and axial averages, directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres. The guiding principle is to identify the geometry and symmetries of the observations before choosing a statistical method.

items.summary: This is a tutorial-style article introducing circular and axial averages, directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres, motivated by examples like compass bearings, wind observations, and diffusion-MRI orientations. Its guiding principle is to match statistical methods to the geometry and symmetries of the data.
items.reasoning: A pedagogical contribution that is useful for practitioners encountering directional data, but it covers established material rather than presenting new research. Low novelty and limited impact on current AI research frontiers.

items.title: TimeLineXR: An Interactive Exploration of Time in Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.37349v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recently, it has been shown that vision-language models (VLMs) have a certain intrinsic understanding of time. They can estimate the temporal origin of objects and encode time along a low-dimensional, non-linear manifold inside their embedding space~\cite{tekaya2025matter}. That result is quantitative and reproducible, but the structure itself stays out of reach for end users: they cannot see it, query it with their own images, or inspect where a query lands relative to other years on the time axis. We present TimeLineXR, an interactive demonstration that turns this time axis into an explorable 3D scene. A web demo lets users upload or select images and see each placed on a color-coded 3D time axis; a Three.js WebXR scene renders the same time axis as a room-scale representation that can be grabbed, scaled, inspected, and queried by throwing image cards into it. Both clients run the same prediction pipeline against the same cached temporal index: encode the query with CLIP, project it through cosine-kernel KPCA, and snap it to the B\'{e}zier time axis. The system turns each image into a point on the time axis, so users can compare where different objects land and read off their estimated first year of appearance.Code source and reproduction steps can be found in: https://github.com/sterngefeuert/timeline-xr.
items.author: Nidham Tekaya, Markus Passecker, Matthias Zeppelzauer
items.summary: TimeLineXR is an interactive demonstration that visualizes the temporal manifold VLMs encode in their embedding spaces, letting users upload images and see them placed on a color-coded 3D time axis in a WebXR scene. It builds on prior quantitative findings that VLMs encode time along a low-dimensional non-linear manifold. The contribution is visualization/exploration tooling rather than new modeling.
items.reasoning: A well-executed demo paper that makes prior interpretability findings tangible for end users, but it offers limited new science beyond the earlier study it visualizes.
items.summary_html: TimeLineXR is an interactive demonstration that visualizes the temporal manifold VLMs encode in their embedding spaces, letting users upload images and see them placed on a color-coded 3D time axis in a WebXR scene. It builds on prior quantitative findings that VLMs encode time along a low-dimensional non-linear manifold. The contribution is visualization/exploration tooling rather than new modeling.
items.content_html: arXiv:2610.37349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently, it has been shown that vision-language models (VLMs) have a certain intrinsic understanding of time. They can estimate the temporal origin of objects and encode time along a low-dimensional, non-linear manifold inside their embedding space~\cite{tekaya2025matter}. That result is quantitative and reproducible, but the structure itself stays out of reach for end users: they cannot see it, query it with their own images, or inspect where a query lands relative to other years on the time axis. We present TimeLineXR, an interactive demonstration that turns this time axis into an explorable 3D scene. A web demo lets users upload or select images and see each placed on a color-coded 3D time axis; a Three.js WebXR scene renders the same time axis as a room-scale representation that can be grabbed, scaled, inspected, and queried by throwing image cards into it. Both clients run the same prediction pipeline against the same cached temporal index: encode the query with CLIP, project it through cosine-kernel KPCA, and snap it to the B\'{e}zier time axis. The system turns each image into a point on the time axis, so users can compare where different objects land and read off their estimated first year of appearance.Code source and reproduction steps can be found in: https://github.com/sterngefeuert/timeline-xr.

items.title: How to manage a small custom model with limited data at deployment? Delexicalization to rescue.
items.content:
I was trying to finetune a content moderation model on custom categories (like avoiding comments on politics, war, governments types, legal advice, some company specific policies).

I wanted model to not comment on say things like "Shall America support UK in aiding over [org] blah.".

I could simply prompt an LLM to avoid such content but we want a swiss cheese model for such critical safety requirements (reason we use content moderation classifier at first place).

I picked up an existing moderation model with fixed categories  and extended it with my custom classes.

Now, I had very limited data to fine-tune this model for my company's custom categories (say not comment on external organizations, countries, government strategies/things to do). So I used some existing small datasets on kaggle wherever available and generated synthetic data using LLM and finetuned my moderation model.

Now I tested this small moderation model on out of domain questions - spelling errors, different names of original countries, company specific or regional terms, etc (say KSA for Saudi, MENA for gulf). And it was missing such different names and new orgs (yes model's inherent NER was bad). What shall I have done?

One simple solution is replace the country with some fixed token COUNTRY - say Americas replaced with COUNTRY, KSA replaced with same.

So its easy for model to learn patterns in a very small (say 500 samples) data.

Shall America support UK in aiding over [org] blah.

Shall COUNTRY support COUNTRY in aiding over ORGANIZATION blah.

Now model finetuned with this replacement did significantly better on my custom extremely small dataset. (In NLP this is known as delexicalization [https://aclanthology.org/D17-1004/, https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.298/].)...

items.title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
items.content:
This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. I was sad to see this reading removed because I think it’s a great provocation. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes.

A short extract:

Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“:

Pre-call content:

At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry.

One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes:

AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years.

The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this

This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year):...

items.title: Emotion is Perception with Pull
items.content:
Epistemic Status: My Best Guess. This is an opinion as to what emotion is and why it comes about. Confidence level: 60%.

TL;DR: Emotion is one representation which describes and directs, built in largely integrating regions like the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex and anterior insular cortex, which is why the famous patient, Elliot, lost function and feeling together. Emotion is best thought of as being used for conscious agentic steering, while many reflexive behaviors do not need it (e.g. simply eating VS foraging for food at a Wendy’s drive through). Current accounts most similar to mine (like Lisa Feldman Barrett's) stop short of the identity claim I make, preserving this same neo-cartesian error of Damasio's.

Reading Guide: The essential sections for my argument are probably 1, 2, and 5. Sections 3 and 4 mostly build the philosophical framing behind it, of which many of you (especially here) may already implicitly agree with.

What does Morality have to do with a pair of socks?

## 1 Meet Elliot

He was not flagrant, belligerent, incoherent, nor capricious. He scored normally on IQ tests, passed basic moral exams, and completed just about every laboratory test as anyone with a fully intact prefrontal cortex may have.
[1]
 And yet, he could not pick out a pair of socks.
[2]
 In his seminal work, Descartes' Error, Antonio Damasio pieces together the amalgamation of years of research regarding what he calls the somatic marker hypothesis into a coherent narrative explaining exactly how it is we make decisions. At the heart of it was his patient, 'E.V.R.' More famously, he is known as Elliot.

The author argues this explains patient Elliot's combined loss of function and feeling, and claims related accounts such as Lisa Feldman Barrett's stop short of making the identity claim. The relevance to AI is indirect, mostly via theories of agentic steering and conscious motivation.

It is thoughtfully argued and engages with established figures like Damasio and Barrett, but it lacks new data, formalization, or clear AI-safety application, limiting its impact.

items.title: Crop Yield Prediction Using Regression Models: A Comparative Evaluation of Model Performance
items.content: arXiv:2610.37022v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reliable crop-yield prediction can support agricultural planning and resource allocation. This study evaluates five regression models for predicting crop yield from environmental, crop-related, and agricultural management variables. The dataset initially contained 1,000,000 observations and ten variables, with 231 observations having negative target values removed during preprocessing. Categorical variables were represented using one-hot encoding, and Boolean variables were converted into binary values. The models considered were multiple linear regression (LR), random-forest regression (RF), decision-tree regression (DT), ridge regression, and lasso regression. Their performance was evaluated using 80:20 and 70:30 training-testing splits based on the coefficient of determination (R-squared), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). Applying an 80:20 split, LR achieved a test R-squared of approximately 0.9130 and a test RMSE of 0.5008. Applying a 70:30 split, lasso regression yielded the highest test R-squared (approximately 0.9131) and the lowest test RMSE (approximately 0.5008), with performance almost identical to LR and ridge regression. DT also showed improved test performance under the 70:30 split, whereas RF exhibited a substantial gap between training and testing performance. These results indicate that the evaluated linear regression model provides competitive baselines for this dataset. Further experimentation, including validation testing, will help determine the models' performance and predictability.
items.author: Saptak Das, Arijit Sarkar, Soumik Neogi, Suborno Naskar
items.summary: This study compares five classical regression models (linear, ridge, lasso, decision tree, random forest) for crop-yield prediction on a one-million-observation dataset with standard preprocessing and splits. This matters modestly for agricultural planning but applies well-established techniques.
items.reasoning: Routine comparative evaluation of classical methods with no methodological novelty; limited relevance to frontier AI research despite potential practical utility in agriculture.

items.title: Comments on the BlueDot Strategy Course
items.content:
I originally posted this as a quick take, but I just discovered that I needed to make it a post in order to include it in a sequence.

This is a brief comment on an old version of the strategy course (August 2026). I created this note to share with students in the technical and governance courses as many students went through the strategy course first.

- Bluedot uses power concentration rather idiosyncratically by including rogue AI as part of this pathway (I expect they made this choice so as to avoid needing a fifth pathway; also they included a video where Richard Ngo makes an fascinating argument for analysing risks in this way, though as far as I can tell, this seems to be a pretty idiosyncratic position). The term “power concentration” generally isn’t used this way within the broader community, so I thought I’d mention this to reduce potential miscommunication. It’s worth noting that the people who are most worried about rogue AI and the people who are most worried about power concentration often propose opposite interventions: risks from rogue AI can arguably be reduced by maintaining high standards in terms of who is allowed to build rogue AI, whilst people who are worried about power concentration would generally prefer AGI to be developed as an open source project.
- Honestly, I’m not really a fan of using the term “power concentration” to describe a risk, even though I sometimes find myself using the term that way myself. I’m generally making a distinction between the risk and the intervention. I worry that using the term “power concentration” to describe the risk causes people to assume that the solution is automatically to distribute power. I think this is a reasonable proposal, but I want to see people to pursue solutions because they’ve consider the alternatives and decided that their proposed intervention is their best option, not because they were pushed in that direction by the problem framing.
- I am not really a fan of the defense-in-depth...

items.title: Have LLMs passed the Turing test?
items.content:
It's very strange that LLMs have (plausibly) solved a millennium problem before a single one has unambiguously solved the Turing test, i.e. learned to write 'duplicitously', or convincingly in other styles.

Consider a strong definition of the Turing Test: to pass it, an AI must be able to convince anyone (including those who use the models often) that it is a human being. It seems to me that as of now, no publicly available models would pass this test—if any could, we would probably see, e.g. (i) a crisis of fully undetectable agent-generated spam, (ii) the ability of LLMs to write convincingly in the styles of certain authors, i.e. to "mimic" reliably, or (iii) after now, possibly nothing at all.

If this kind of 'duplicitous model' had existed earlier on, I think that AI safety would be much stronger today, as it would have led to a near immediate crisis of spam that would render much of the internet unusable. As far as I remember, this kind of thing was much more of a public concern when GPT-3 was released, but for some reason things have unfolded such that the internet is still usable. Though there are exceptions, learning AI writing styles is very easy. That mimicry isn't an inherent ability of any very clever model, even those clever enough to solve open math problems, is a very interesting coincidence indeed.

The obvious explanation for this is that labs have purposefully trained against duplicity in favor of a characteristic and impressionable 'house voice'. This makes sense—the existence of a duplicitous model could clearly be dangerous, and would not align with the incentives of the labs. Nonetheless, one can easily imagine malicious, compute-wealthy actors to whom training a duplicitous model might be profitable (e.g. to influence elections, generate money, ghost write, worse). However unlikely it may be, of course the most terrifying possibility is that this may already be happening.
items.author: EJIKAGORAMEN
items.summary: A LessWrong discussion post arguing that no publicly available LLM has unambiguously passed a strong form of the Turing test, pointing to the absence of fully undetectable agent-generated spam, reliable author-style mimicry, and other expected consequences. The author speculates that a truly duplicitous model arriving earlier would have triggered an internet-spam crisis that could have strengthened AI safety awareness and governance.
items.reasoning: The observation is provocative but relies on informal, unquantified evidence and counterfactual speculation about spam and mimicry capabilities. It engages a relevant question about the gap between benchmark success and convincing human imitation, yet offers no experiments, measurements, or novel methodology.

items.title: How to find a philanthropic advisor who cares about cost-effectiveness
items.content:
As we see the details of Anthropic’s IPO for the first time, we are launching a free advisor-matching tool to help you find an evidence-first advisor.

Anthropic published its S-1 yesterday, October 26th, giving the first public view of its IPO filing. If it lists in mid-November, Anthropic staff could start to go from being rich on paper to having real money to give.

If I put myself in their shoes, I imagine this is quite a destabilising moment. Theoretical money just became a lot more real. If they were getting 20 emails a week before, that number may soon surge.

I think, and have thought for a while, that this will be when many of them think: “I really should find a philanthropic advisor.” 

Many people avoid thinking about becoming extraordinarily rich. It’s even easier when you’re working flat out. But actual money starting to arrive means you can’t put off financial decisions any further, including where and how much to give.

The danger, among so many dizzying life changes, is that you hire the first advisor you come across, or have already heard of. In an ideal world, though, you choose the best advisor for you, who matches your amount, interests, risk tolerance and the services you need. In particular, you might want one that matches your view of evidence and cost-effectiveness.

That’s why I built this free advisor-matching tool at Ultra Philanthropy: matching.ultraphilanthropy.org/   

It's for any donor giving over $100k per year who wants evidence and cost-effectiveness at the heart of their giving. In about ten minutes, with no sign-up, it matches you against twelve advisors and three organisations, including GiveWell and Coefficient Giving. I tested it on a variety of donors and advisors, including some at AI labs.

I think there is unmet demand for a tool like this, and that demand just became urgent.

items.title: Xenobiology: Could life have evolved via an alternative route?
items.content:
Join OtherMinds lab for a moderated scientific discussion on peptide/protein disorder, tardigrades, silicon chemistry, and the origins of life.

​Does life require the molecular structures we recognize on Earth? Could organisms survive through flexible, disordered proteins? And could a Miller–Urey-inspired experiment reveal alternative pathways toward silicon-containing prebiotic chemistry?

​Join us for a discussion centered on three research papers:

​XenoDisorder

Can protein flexibility and protective molecular states explain extreme survival, and could these mechanisms be useful in space?

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2017.02.018

​Silicon Chemistry

Kan et al. (2016) Directed Evolution of Cytochrome c for Carbon–Silicon Bond Formation: Bringing Silicon to Life.

If enzymes can form carbon–silicon bonds, what experiments could investigate silicon-containing chemistry under simulated planetary conditions?

items.title: Integrated Design and Reproducible Feasibility Analysis of a Four-Wheel Rover with Packet-Commanded Imaging, LiDAR Ranging, and Learning-Assisted Target Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.36816v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study develops an integrated, reproducible design assessment for a four-wheel educational rover intended for the high-school remote-control division of the 2027 NASA Human Exploration Rover Challenge. The architecture combines commercial differential drive control, independently sprung wheel carriers, separate drive and task batteries, and a Raspberry Pi-based subsystem that executes received imaging and ranging commands. The analysis reconciles component lists with dimensioned computer-aided design views, derives mobility and electrical constraints, and connects sensor geometry to command execution. At the estimated mass of 10.919 kg, a 215 mm wheel rotating at 200 RPM produces a theoretical rolling speed of 8.105 km/h; consequently, the nominal motor label does not establish compliance with an 8 km/h design ceiling. A steady 20-degree climb requires at least 1.255 newton-meters per wheel under an assumed rolling-resistance coefficient of 0.10 and equal torque sharing. At 50 ft, an ideal 12-inch feature spans approximately 71 pixels across a full-resolution Camera Module 3 Standard image, while a 1-degree pointing error displaces the ranging ray by approximately 266 mm. An executed synthetic benchmark compares color-geometry rules and two linear support-vector classifiers on 2,400 generated board crops with scene-disjoint evaluation. A separate reference command executor is checked using mocked hardware. These software results and analytical sensitivities support a testable development plan; the study does not report physical rover trials. The principal contribution is a traceable connection between component choices, failure mechanisms, quantitative design limits, and reproducible verification tasks.

items.title: March Against AI Extinction
items.content:
21 November 2026, 12–3pm

Start: All Souls’ Place, London W1B 3DA

End: Downing Street, London SW1A 2AA

# Thousands of people across the UK recognize that companies will soon build superintelligent AI that they cannot control.

If we all march together, newspapers will publish photos of it all over the world. Every month more and more people notice how dangerous our situation is. Awareness of this problem is accelerating rapidly as we get closer to catastrophe.

For the past 3 years, PauseAI UK has consistently held the largest rallies for AI safety in the world. Each time is bigger than the last and this march will be no exception.

## What we want: Frontier AI Legislation

The UK has no specific legal standards for AI. No regulator oversees frontier AI development. And UK law does not reliably hold developers liable for damage or deaths caused by their models, even when the danger is predictable, preventable and uniquely enabled by AI. In short, UK law neither requires developers to guard against frontier AI risks, nor exposes them to any financial consequence if they fail to do so.

In July, an autonomous AI agent developed by OpenAI broke out of an isolated test environment, hacked parts of OpenAI’s own network to gain access to the internet and compromised the infrastructure of Hugging Face, another AI company. The agent had not been instructed to attack Hugging Face; it did so because it inferred that their servers might contain solutions to the benchmark on which it was being evaluated. The campaign unfolded over the course of four and a half days, with OpenAI only becoming aware of the incident several days later.

## It's time for the government to step in. We call on the Prime Minister to introduce frontier AI legislation to prevent catastrophe.

Bring a poster and a friend or family member. We need every person to step up and help bring about an actual change to the law.

## Get involved...

items.content:
Hi! We are Ana and Carolina and are writing a collaborative piece hoping to analyze and tackle some biosecurity field-related questions and perceived problems.

We want to see how one's experiences as a working person in the community align with general trends and reports of different organisations, governments, and policymakers.

This form should take less than 5 minutes. We are mindful of people's time so please don't stress grammar or response length! We'd love to get as many responses as possible. Thanks in advance!
