items.title: Remote embalming and shipment for brain or whole body preservation with Sparks
items.content:
(Cross-posted at the Sparks Newsletter)

Let’s imagine that you think that preservation after legal death with the goal of future revival may actually be able to preserve important information that you care about, such as long-term memories.

Let’s also imagine that, unfortunately, you live far away from an organization that offers these services. In that case, especially if you die suddenly, the chances of having a preservation team get out to you in a timely manner (within <4-12 or even <24 hours) seem quite small.

But what about embalmers? Don’t they already pump aldehyde-containing solutions through the blood vessels of recently deceased people? And aren’t there already a bunch of them in lots of places in the world? Couldn’t they possibly do the initial preservation themselves, thus stabilizing the structure of the brain/body and thereby addressing one of the key problems related to access to preservation services?

This topic has been a hotly debated one over the years in the field of preservation/biostasis/cryonics. Of course, I will not end the debate in this one essay. But what I will try to do is:

(a) make the case that using the services of embalmers actually does make sense in some circumstances, and then

(b) discuss some practicalities of how people can use the services of remote embalmers to access preservation services with Sparks (where, as a form of disclosure if you were not already aware, I work as a Research Scientist).

Is the use of commercial embalming fluids a good idea for structural brain preservation? The extant evidence is pretty unclear, but it suggests that cellular structure is preserved, as would be expected by the fact that embalming fluids use formaldehyde as their key component...

items.summary: An essay arguing that ordinary embalmers distributed worldwide could perform initial aldehyde-based preservation for biostasis patients far from cryonics facilities, addressing the critical time window after death. The author makes the case for using existing embalming infrastructure and discusses longstanding debates in the preservation community.
items.reasoning: A considered treatment of a practical access problem in biostasis/cryonics, adjacent to long-termist interests in information preservation. The topic is speculative and niche, and the post is advocacy/analysis rather than empirical research.

items.title: Against Girardian mimesis
items.content:
Wikipedia summarizes René Girard's mimetic theory like this:

Man is the creature who does not know what to desire, and he turns to others in order to make up his mind. We desire what others desire because we imitate their desires.

In other words, you think you want something for your own internal reasons, but the actual reason you want it is that someone else wants it, and that makes you desire the thing and compete for it.

The "someone else" whose desires you copy is someone you care about. It could be a friend, a sibling, or a colleague. It could also be a famous person, or even a fictional character. (Not a stranger you don't care about.)

This creates unnecessary social conflict, as people gradually converge on wanting the same thing, people start seeing each other as rivals, this attitude gets copied too, then people start hating each other, but who hates whom gets copied too, until everyone synchronizes at hating one specific person... and then they typically murder the person, and everyone feels happy about the conflict being resolved.

The choice of the person to kill is arbitrary, in the sense that the selected person is definitely not responsible for everything they get blamed for. It is typically someone who is a natural target of coordinated hate, such as a stranger, a poor or disabled person. But sometimes it could even be a king.

It is important for the people not to be aware of this mechanism -- the relief only comes from sincerely believing that the scapegoat was responsible for all the problems, and that by killing them the problems will go away.

...and this is supposed to explain the origins of religions. The sacrifices are the ritualized acts of choosing and killing the scapegoat. Christianity reversed the trope by providing the perspective of the victim -- and although it did not stop the burning of witches and lynching completely, it reduced their occurrence by providing sensitivity to the victims....
items.author: Viliam
items.summary: A critical essay examining Rene Girard's mimetic theory of desire and scapegoating, summarizing the framework and pushing back on its claims. The piece is philosophical commentary on social dynamics rather than empirical or technical AI research.
items.reasoning: Thoughtful philosophical discussion relevant to community discourse, but it is not AI research, offers no novel methodology or empirical findings, and its relevance to AI safety is at most indirect via community epistemics.

items.title: Sci.STEPS opens applications for mentors for the 2027 season
items.content:
Sci.STEPS is now accepting mentor applications for a new season! (See this post for a description of the previous season.)

Sci.STEPS is a free, volunteer-run online mentorship program for early-career researchers, with an AI Safety division alongside STEM fields. As in previous seasons, the season runs February–April 2027, and mentors commit to a minimum of 2 hours per month for 3 months.

Every season, each mentor-mentee pair meets six times over three months. Mentors share their experience, guidance and support with early-career researchers facing a career decision or transition. It is also a chance to give back and to meet motivated people at the start of their careers. 

In addition, Sci.STEPS offers optional webinars on general career development topics such as CV writing, mental health, and coaching.

Participants across all divisions gave the program a 9.8/10 approval rating.

Last season, we piloted an AI Safety division. We had only two mentors in the field but received multiple mentee applications, and the two selected mentees told us the experience was highly useful.

We’d love to have more mentors this season. More mentors means we can support more mentees, and it would also let us launch an AI Safety pod. We’ve already tried the pod model in other disciplines (for example, a sci-comm pod). Participants meet as a group, network, brainstorm career approaches, and work on a small group project. The pod includes all AI Safety mentors and mentees and usually meets biweekly. It is voluntary and in addition to the 1:1 pairings: mentors only commit to the six 1:1 meetings. The model has been highly successful elsewhere, but it needs enough participants to work: a pod works best with 6–10 people, and since not everyone joins, we would ideally have 5–7 AI Safety mentors. We expect to find mentees for them, as last season we received significantly more mentee applications than there were mentors....

items.title: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights
items.content:
Like many leaders today, Prabha Jha has been feeling the significant impact artificial intelligence is having on business operations. While the rapid evolution of the technology can bring fear, uncertainty, and confusion, Jha chose a different response: excitement. She began asking herself, “How do I become part of this once-in-a-lifetime thing?” 

Jha holds a bachelor’s degree in information technology from the University of Calcutta and earned her MBA while working at Verizon, where she continues to build her career. As she looked for an educational opportunity to engage more deeply with AI, MIT quickly emerged as a natural choice. 

Growing up, Jha viewed MIT as “the mecca for anybody who is in engineering and technology,” so she naturally turned to the Institute when seeking an opportunity to learn about AI. Unlike other programs that took place fully online, MIT xPRO’s AI for Senior Executives stood out to Jha primarily because it offered an in-person component that allowed her to meet and connect with peers. 

Jha decided to take the leap. She acknowledges that the program was a significant investment of both time and money, but ultimately views it as one of “the best decisions [she] made” — one she “would do all over again if [she] had to.” The experience gave Jha the opportunity she was looking for to invest in herself and strengthen her skills in AI. It also provided her with invaluable professional relationships and the confidence to develop multiple AI solutions for Verizon. Putting those news skills and relationships to work, she co-wrote, with some of her peers, “The AI Anthology,” a collection of AI insights designed to support other leaders navigating similar challenges with AI. 

An unexpected learning obstacle

Jha’s learning journey wasn’t without its curveballs, though. Just two months before she was set to complete the program, she spent two weeks in the hospital with a severe infection and was unable to graduate with her original cohort. With the help of MIT staff, she joined the next cohort, giving her an unexpected opportunity to spend another five days on campus with 100 brand-new peers. 

“You just never know what curveball life can throw and what it might be there for,” Jha says.

What initially felt like a setback turned into an unexpected benefit. Jha valued the opportunity to meet new people and spend more time on campus. She also appreciated that just six months later, the program’s content had already been refreshed. Those additional “five days of immersion” became a vital part of Jha’s learning journey, giving her and her peers more time to collaborate face-to-face and learn from one another. 

“I think it was eye-opening to be able to meet so many people with diverse backgrounds and geography, and then we connected at the human level,” she says. 

Jha particularly valued that sense of connection in the context of learning about AI, a field that, she acknowledges, comes with fears, vulnerabilities, and difficult questions. Learning alongside peers with different professional and cultural backgrounds gave her new perspectives and added another dimension to the experience. Jha estimates that “30 percent of what I was learning was from the program, material, and professor [while] 70 percent was my peers and the interactions.”

Peer discussions spark an idea

The idea that would change the trajectory of Jha’s time in the program came during a “salon gathering” at the home of Manolis Kellis, a professor in MIT’s Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. As students shared personal stories about their experiences with AI, one story in particular stayed with Jha: that of one of her peers, whose motivation to explore AI solutions stemmed from her work to find a cure for her mother’s Alzheimer's disease and dementia. 

At that moment, Jha realized that AI is personal. She still “gets goosebumps thinking of that moment where AI really became human and a connecting point.”

She saw the value in capturing these diverse perspectives and experiences with AI that go beyond operational efficiency and revenue growth, and wanted to continue the conversation beyond the program. Jha expressed to her peers an interest in capturing these stories and connections in a book. One year later, Jha and 20 other leaders released “The AI Anthology,” a collection of essays examining the influence AI has had across industries and across society. 

One of the biggest takeaways from the AI for Senior Executives program — and one that Jha hopes readers will take from her book — is the importance of thinking differently. 

Jha believes leaders may be missing a fundamental shift: “We are still kind of stuck in this traditional measurement of success,” she says. “We cherish revenue; we like cost-cutting and time-saving, and converting them to dollars.” 

While Jha acknowledges this mindset makes sense in corporate America, she believes leaders must move beyond it in order to find more empowerment through AI and its capabilities. She notes that future generations are already asking different questions, including: “What can I get in the quality of my life?” and “How can I use my time in a way that is fulfilling for me early on?” 

The future of embracing AI for business and a better world 

Jha recognizes that AI adoption is not optional for businesses, and that everyone must learn about and embrace it. At the same time, she is a steadfast believer in AI’s ability to create a better world. Instead of viewing AI as a foregone burden, she sees it as a “transformation unlike any other” that is providing us with the opportunity to overcome insecurity, adapt and grow, and invest in ourselves. 

In her work at Verizon, Jha takes seriously the company’s role as “a brand name for reliable, quality service” providing “critical infrastructure” to groups, such as first responders or children, who depend on their services. This responsibility comes with a privileged obligation to participate in and protect society, and Jha finds it empowering that AI can help enable this. In her own experience, she’s appreciated the ability to accelerate progress and impact, when she may have previously needed to rely on a larger team. 

So, what’s next for Jha? Currently, she is working on a new initiative focused on supporting small and medium-sized businesses that are navigating AI implementation. Her goal is to help them understand what tools they need, how AI fits into their specific operational model, and how they can measure success, so they can focus on their strengths as a business and how they can drive value.

The piece covers her motivations and experience rather than any technical or research content.
items.content_html:
Like many leaders today, Prabha Jha has been feeling the significant impact artificial intelligence is having on business operations. While the rapid evolution of the technology can bring fear, uncertainty, and confusion, Jha chose a different response: excitement. She began asking herself, “How do I become part of this once-in-a-lifetime thing?”

Jha holds a bachelor’s degree in information technology from the University of Calcutta and earned her MBA while working at Verizon, where she continues to build her career. As she looked for an educational opportunity to engage more deeply with AI, MIT quickly emerged as a natural choice.

Growing up, Jha viewed MIT as “the mecca for anybody who is in engineering and technology,” so she naturally turned to the Institute when seeking an opportunity to learn about AI. Unlike other programs that took place fully online, MIT xPRO’s AI for Senior Executives stood out to Jha primarily because it offered an in-person component that allowed her to meet and connect with peers.

Jha decided to take the leap. She acknowledges that the program was a significant investment of both time and money, but ultimately views it as one of “the best decisions [she] made” — one she “would do all over again if [she] had to.” The experience gave Jha the opportunity she was looking for to invest in herself and strengthen her skills in AI. It also provided her with invaluable professional relationships and the confidence to develop multiple AI solutions for Verizon. Putting those news skills and relationships to work, she co-wrote, with some of her peers, “The AI Anthology,” a collection of AI insights designed to support other leaders navigating similar challenges with AI.

An unexpected learning obstacle

Jha’s learning journey wasn’t without its curveballs, though. Just two months before she was set to complete the program, she spent two weeks in the hospital with a severe infection and was unable to graduate with her original cohort. With the help of MIT staff, she joined the next cohort, giving her an unexpected opportunity to spend another five days on campus with 100 brand-new peers.

“You just never know what curveball life can throw and what it might be there for,” Jha says.

What initially felt like a setback turned into an unexpected benefit. Jha valued the opportunity to meet new people and spend more time on campus. She also appreciated that just six months later, the program’s content had already been refreshed. Those additional “five days of immersion” became a vital part of Jha’s learning journey, giving her and her peers more time to collaborate face-to-face and learn from one another.

“I think it was eye-opening to be able to meet so many people with diverse backgrounds and geography, and then we connected at the human level,” she says.

Jha particularly valued that sense of connection in the context of learning about AI, a field that, she acknowledges, comes with fears, vulnerabilities, and difficult questions. Learning alongside peers with different professional and cultural backgrounds gave her new perspectives and added another dimension to the experience. Jha estimates that “30 percent of what I was learning was from the program, material, and professor [while] 70 percent was my peers and the interactions.”

Peer discussions spark an idea

The idea that would change the trajectory of Jha’s time in the program came during a “salon gathering” at the home of Manolis Kellis, a professor in MIT’s Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. As students shared personal stories about their experiences with AI, one story in particular stayed with Jha: that of one of her peers, whose motivation to explore AI solutions stemmed from her work to find a cure for her mother’s Alzheimer's disease and dementia.

At that moment, Jha realized that AI is personal. She still “gets goosebumps thinking of that moment where AI really became human and a connecting point.”

She saw the value in capturing these diverse perspectives and experiences with AI that go beyond operational efficiency and revenue growth, and wanted to continue the conversation beyond the program. Jha expressed to her peers an interest in capturing these stories and connections in a book. One year later, Jha and 20 other leaders released “The AI Anthology,” a collection of essays examining the influence AI has had across industries and across society.

One of the biggest takeaways from the AI for Senior Executives program — and one that Jha hopes readers will take from her book — is the importance of thinking differently.

Jha believes leaders may be missing a fundamental shift: “We are still kind of stuck in this traditional measurement of success,” she says. “We cherish revenue; we like cost-cutting and time-saving, and converting them to dollars.”

While Jha acknowledges this mindset makes sense in corporate America, she believes leaders must move beyond it in order to find more empowerment through AI and its capabilities. She notes that future generations are already asking different questions, including: “What can I get in the quality of my life?” and “How can I use my time in a way that is fulfilling for me early on?”

The future of embracing AI for business and a better world

Jha recognizes that AI adoption is not optional for businesses, and that everyone must learn about and embrace it. At the same time, she is a steadfast believer in AI’s ability to create a better world. Instead of viewing AI as a foregone burden, she sees it as a “transformation unlike any other” that is providing us with the opportunity to overcome insecurity, adapt and grow, and invest in ourselves.

In her work at Verizon, Jha takes seriously the company’s role as “a brand name for reliable, quality service” providing “critical infrastructure” to groups, such as first responders or children, who depend on their services. This responsibility comes with a privileged obligation to participate in and protect society, and Jha finds it empowering that AI can help enable this. In her own experience, she’s appreciated the ability to accelerate progress and impact, when she may have previously needed to rely on a larger team.

So, what’s next for Jha? Currently, she is working on a new initiative focused on supporting small and medium-sized businesses that are navigating AI implementation. Her goal is to help them understand what tools they need, how AI fits into their specific operational model, and how they can measure success, so they can focus on their strengths as a business and how they can drive value.
